Belle Boyd. A Confederate spy and intelligence operative during the American Civil War, known for using her charm and social access to extract military information from Union officers. Operating in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, she gathered intelligence for Confederate General Thomas Jackson, known as Stonewall Jackson. She earned the nickname La Belle Rebelle for her daring and fearlessness.

Belle Boyd was born in Martinsburg, Virginia, in eighteen forty-four into an aristocratic planter family with strong secessionist sympathies. She began her intelligence work early in the war by gathering information from Union soldiers quartered near her family's home and passing it to Confederate commanders. She used social events, flirtation, and her position as a trusted member of the community to gain access to Union officers' plans and movements without arousing suspicion.

She provided crucial intelligence about Union troop strength and positions to Confederate forces, particularly during the Shenandoah Valley campaign of eighteen sixty-two. But her espionage activities were eventually discovered. Union authorities arrested her in eighteen sixty-two and imprisoned her in Old Capitol Prison in Washington, District of Columbia. She was later released in a prisoner exchange, though her freedom did not last.

She continued her intelligence work after her release, eventually arrested again in eighteen sixty-four. She spent the remainder of the war in exile or under detention. After the war, she became a public figure, writing memoirs, performing on stage, and capitalizing on her notoriety. She died in Wisconsin in nineteen hundred, remembered as one of the most celebrated female intelligence agents of the Civil War era.
